query: Earlier efforts have produced HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations and have used thermophysical-parameter calculations, CALPHAD, first-principles calculations, and machine-learning modeling to identify promising alloys. However, large computational demands and low efficiency impede rapid discovery, while fracture properties such as toughness remain difficult to predict. For HfNbTiVAl10 in its reported hierarchical-heterostructured state, what single testable methodological hypothesis could overcome these limitations for predicting Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness under tensile and fracture testing? Explain the rationale, quantify the expected gains in accuracy and efficiency over prior methods, specify the conditions under which it would cease to be reliable, identify supporting prior evidence, and define a blinded prospective benchmark that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid, physics‐informed machine learning framework—one that extracts key microstructural descriptors from limited-scale first‐principles calculations and microstructural imaging of the HfNbTiVAl10 hierarchical heterostructure—can be used to rapidly predict its Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness with comparable accuracy to full-scale CALPHAD/DFT methods but with drastically reduced computational cost.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 in its reported hierarchical‐heterostructured state featuring multilevel chemical and compositional fluctuations.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy a surrogate modeling approach that first quantifies mesoscale descriptors (such as local chemical inhomogeneities, short‐range order metrics, and grain boundary characteristics) via targeted first‐principles calculations and microstructural characterization, and then integrates these features into a machine learning model trained to predict elastic modulus, yield strength, and toughness under tensile/fracture conditions.
generation.conditions: The predictions will be evaluated under simulated or experimentally validated tensile and fracture testing conditions at room (and optionally elevated) temperatures, where the hierarchical structure governs deformation and crack-propagation.
generation.structural_mediator: The multilevel chemical fluctuations and hierarchical structural features mediate local stress distributions and defect interactions, thereby influencing both elastic and inelastic (yield and fracture) behavior.
generation.mechanism: By capturing the key mesoscale and atomistic structural features that drive deformation mechanisms (e.g., dislocation emission, crack initiation and bridging) in the heterogeneous alloy, the ML model can learn robust structure–property relationships. This reduces the need for exhaustive, computation-intensive simulations while simultaneously providing predictions for traditionally elusive fracture toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: The framework is expected to reduce computational costs by one to two orders of magnitude and achieve prediction errors below ~20% for Young’s modulus and yield strength, while providing improved, though still preliminary, estimates for fracture toughness relative to existing methods.
generation.baseline: Prior approaches relying solely on full-scale CALPHAD, first-principles, or MD simulations that are both computationally demanding and inefficient, and which have limited success in predicting toughness.
generation.boundary: The method’s reliability may deteriorate if the hierarchical heterostructural features in new samples significantly deviate from those in the training set or if the deformation mechanisms change under conditions (e.g., extreme temperatures or loading rates) not represented in the model’s development.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative gains in accuracy for fracture toughness predictions remain somewhat uncertain due to sparse training data on crack propagation in hierarchical heterostructures; further empirical validation is required.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple HfNbTiVAl10 samples that exhibit the reported hierarchical heterostructure. Perform detailed microstructural characterization (using TEM, APT, etc.) to extract the defined descriptors. Train the physics‐informed ML model with these descriptors and predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness. Then, conduct standardized tensile and fracture tests on the same samples to obtain independent experimental measurements.
measurements: Young’s modulus via resonant ultrasound or nanoindentation
Yield strength from standard tensile tests
Microstructural descriptors including grain size, local chemical fluctuation metrics, and short-range order parameters
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML predictions deviate by more than 20% on average from the experimental measurements for any of the mechanical properties across multiple, independently prepared samples, or if the model fails to capture systematic trends linked to controlled variations in microstructure, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The following design criteria for the selection of best HEA compositions were considered: (1) high energetical stability, (2) lightweight, (3) large elastic modulus, (4) large specific stiffness, and (5) high Pugh’s ratio (which indicates the alloy ductility vs. its brittleness). The five topmost compositions were selected according to the design criteria for each of the three HEA families. The present work, for the first time, employed HT and HF first-principles-based methods to design lightweight HEAs. It is widely acknowledged that designing and fabricating lightweight HEAs with stable structures and superior mechanical properties remains a challenge. Our study reveals that HEAs with the topmost compositions exhibit a negative formation energy, low mass density and high specific Young’s modulus, but a low Pugh’s ratio. These results indicate that the designed lightweight HEAs can be energetically more stable, lighter, and stiffer compared to existing Al alloys. However, they may exhibit a low ductility. These findings will provide valuable insights and guidance for experimental development and fabrication of lightweight HEAs with desirable properties.

The D parameter is a critical metric for predicting the room-temperature ductility of body-centered cubic (BCC) high-entropy alloys (HEAs). This parameter arises from analyzing the competition at the nanoscale between cleavage and dislocation emission at sharp crack tips. Based on an earlier work of Mak et al. [], Hu et al. [] proposed that BCC multicomponent alloys with a higher D=γsfγusf ratio are more likely to demonstrate inherent ductility. Here, γusf is the unstable stacking fault energy, and γs is the surface energy. A lower γusf makes it easier to emit dislocations, rendering the alloy to exhibit ductility. By employing first-principles calculations to construct surrogate models, they observed a positive correlation between the D parameter and experimentally observed plasticity across various measurements. The D parameter must be computed to integrate it into the machine learning models. We utilize the Effective Medium Calculation (EMC) method [] to reduce computational burden while maintaining fidelity to experimental and Density Functional Theory (DFT)-calculated values. AbstractThe aim of this work was to provide a guidance to the prediction and design of high-entropy alloys with good performance. New promising compositions of refractory high-entropy alloys with the desired phase composition and mechanical properties (yield strength) have been predicted using a combination of machine learning, phenomenological rules and CALPHAD modeling. The yield strength prediction in a wide range of temperatures (20–800 °C) was made using a surrogate model based on a support-vector machine algorithm. The yield strength at 20 °C and 600 °C was predicted quite precisely (the average prediction error was 11% and 13.5%, respectively) with a decrease in the precision to slightly higher than 20% at 800 °C. An Al13Cr12Nb20Ti20V35 alloy with an excellent combination of ductility and yield strength at 20 °C (16.6% and 1295 MPa, respectively) and at 800 °C (more 50% and 898 MPa, respectively) was produced based on the prediction.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, machine learning, prediction, strength, structure
